newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy court ponders war trial for ex-SS major Hass.
newsitem.headline: Italy court ponders war trial for ex-SS major Hass.

text.p: An Italian military court opened a hearing on Thursday to decide whether sufficient evidence existed to try former SS major Karl Hass for war crimes for his involvement in a World War Two Nazi massacre.
Hass, 84, attended the closed-door committal hearing presided over by preliminary hearing judge Giuseppe Mazzi, but made no comment to journalists outside the courtroom.

Military prosecutors have said they want to try Hass with former SS captain Erich Priebke, who faces re-trial over his involvement in the March 1944 massacre in which the SS killed 335 men and boys in the Ardeatine Caves outside of Rome.
The SS ordered the massacre in retaliation for a partisan bomb attack in Rome which killed 33 soldiers of German occupying troops.
Civil plaintiff lawyers, representing relatives of the victims, said they had asked Mazzi to move the Hass case to a civilian court, arguing the military court had no jurisdiction.
Mazzi did not immediately rule on the request and it was not known when he would decide whether to order a trial.

Hass has been living under police supervision at a clinic near Rome where he is recovering from a fractured pelvis suffered last June when he tried to clamber over a hotel balcony and flee on the eve of testimony as a prosecution witness at Priebke's original trial.
Hass, whose home is in Switzerland, eventually testified from his hospital bed. It was his testimony which prompted prosecutors to seek his indictment on charges of complicity in multiple murder.

Both he and Priebke have each admitted to shooting two of the victims at the caves. They say they were under military orders to participate and would have been killed themselves had they refused to take part.
Italy's highest court, the Court of Cassation, ordered a new trial for Priebke in October, citing irregularities at his first hearing which ended in uproar on August 1.
A three-judge panel decided in a split verdict that while Priebke was guilty of multiple murder he could not be punished because of mitigating circumstances and expiry of a statute of limitations.
Angry protesters laid siege to the military court, trapping Priebke and the judges inside in a stand-off lasting several hours which only ended when Priebke was re-arrested.
